items.passage: Listeners in a study by Courtney Hilton, Cody Moser, and colleagues best identified which recordings of speech and song from 21 societies were directed at infants when the language was one they spoke, a pattern that might suggest the skill is ______ comprehension of the words. Yet even recordings in languages from unrelated families were classified correctly at rates exceeding chance.
items.explanation: Contingent on means depending on. The listeners did best “when the language was one they spoke,” which might make it seem that identifying infant-directed recordings depends on understanding the words. The next sentence, introduced by “Yet,” undercuts that impression: even recordings “in languages from unrelated families were classified correctly at rates exceeding chance.” The blank names the dependence the first pattern suggests.

A.recipe: reversal: the trait of the finding (ANT)
A.why_wrong: Extraneous to means irrelevant to. That describes what the second sentence points toward, not what the first pattern suggests: listeners doing best “when the language was one they spoke” would suggest that comprehension matters, and the “Yet” sentence then pushes back against that suggestion.

C.why_wrong: Synonymous with means the same as. Doing best in a familiar language suggests that comprehension of the words helps with the judgment, not that the judgment and comprehension are one and the same thing.

D.why_wrong: Inimical to means harmful to or opposed to. The pattern described points the other way: listeners did best “when the language was one they spoke,” so nothing suggests that the skill works against comprehension of the words.

band7_moves: concessive frame that hides the direction: the blank sits on what a pattern ‘might suggest’, and the finding that undercuts it comes in the next sentence (Yet ...)
wrong-party reversal: extraneous to names the trait the finding points toward
near miss failing on one feature (synonymous with: identity, not dependence)
all four options past rank 17,000, three past 23,000

sources.what: PMC full text, Hilton, Moser et al. 2022 (Nature Human Behaviour), Acoustic regularities in infant-directed speech and song across cultures: recordings from 21 societies played to 51,065 listeners in 187 countries who guessed whether each was infant-directed; sensitivity significantly above chance in all cases (different language family, same family, same language), with performance increasing with relatedness

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology, music cognition). Key letter B. Steps: 3 (best accuracy in one's own language suggests dependence; the Yet sentence shows success without it; the blank is the suggested dependence, not the finding). Concessive frame: yes. Raw freq.txt ranks: extraneous to 27,907; contingent on 17,762; synonymous with 23,689; inimical to 27,949 (4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000; mean log10 4.37). Band-5 guard: clear (key is the commonest option). Kept to the paper: accuracy did rise with relatedness, so the passage says listeners ‘best identified’ recordings ‘when the language was one they spoke’ and ‘at rates exceeding chance’, never that relatedness made no difference (the abstract’s ‘robust to’ means above chance at every level). Wording kept apart from the live transitions item on cross-cultural emotion recognition (Elfenbein and Ambady), which a check_rw overlap flagged.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

band7.why: Recounted: extraneous to 27,907, contingent on 17,762, synonymous with 23,689, inimical to 27,949 (4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000, mean log10 4.38; combined gate passes; band-5 guard clear, key the commonest). Frame hides the direction (the blank is what a pattern might suggest, undercut by the Yet sentence), as in 3021d9ef; extraneous to is the wrong-party reversal and synonymous with a near miss failing on one feature (identity, not dependence). Band 7.

items.passage: In the 1990s, some academics predicted that Yurok, the ancestral language of a Native nation in northern California, would be extinct by 2010. The language’s ______ has confounded that forecast: although its last native speaker died in 2013 and fluent speakers remain few, hundreds had by then acquired at least a rudimentary knowledge of Yurok, and it has entered the curriculum of several regional high schools.
items.explanation: Tenacity is the quality of holding on firmly and refusing to give way. Academics expected that Yurok “would be extinct by 2010,” but the language has held on: “hundreds had by then acquired at least a rudimentary knowledge of Yurok,” and it “has entered the curriculum of several regional high schools.” Its tenacity, not its disappearance, is what “confounded that forecast.”

A.why_wrong: Obsolescence means passing out of use. That is what the academics predicted, so it would have confirmed the forecast rather than “confounded” it; the text instead describes hundreds of learners and classes in high schools.

B.why_wrong: Prevalence means being widespread or common. The text says that “fluent speakers remain few” and that many learners have only “at least a rudimentary knowledge of Yurok,” so the language has survived without becoming widespread.

C.why_wrong: Opacity means being hard to understand. The text says nothing about Yurok being difficult to grasp, and difficulty would not explain why the prediction that it “would be extinct by 2010” failed.

band7_moves: rare key in a transferred sense (tenacity, usually of a person, here of a language)
clue in a different register from the key (confounded that forecast; hundreds had learned at least some Yurok)
near-synonym distractor failing on one feature: prevalence (survival read as being widespread, ruled out by few fluent speakers)
all four options past rank 14,000, three past 33,000 or unseen

sources.what: Wikipedia, Yurok language: academics in the 1990s predicted it would be extinct by 2010; last native speaker Archie Thompson died March 26, 2013; as of February 2013 over 300 basic speakers and 17 conversationally fluent; as of 2014 taught in four high schools and two elementary schools

items.notes: Subject: social science (linguistics, language revitalization). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (a forecast of extinction failed because the language held on through learners; the blank names that holding on). Transferred-sense key: yes. Raw freq.txt ranks: obsolescence unseen; prevalence 33,822; opacity 67,799; tenacity 14,101 (4 of 4 past 10,000; key the commonest). Revival, resurgence, persistence and survival were not offered (each would also fit). ‘fluent speakers remain few’ (17 conversationally fluent in 2013) is there to rule out prevalence.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

band7.why: Recounted: obsolescence unseen, prevalence 33,822, opacity 67,799, tenacity 14,101 (4 of 4 past 10,000; rarest distractor past 50,000; band-5 guard clear, key the commonest). Key in a transferred sense (tenacity of a language, usually of a person), clue in another register (confounded that forecast; hundreds had learned some Yurok), and prevalence a survival-adjacent near miss killed by fluent speakers remain few, like fecundity against ubiquity in bce4d106. Band 7.

items.passage: Research on autobiographical memory has long concentrated on patients with neurological disease, for whom losing the capacity to vividly recollect personal experiences can be ______. But Daniela Palombo, Brian Levine, and colleagues identified three healthy adults who have always lacked that capacity yet function normally in everyday life, since their learning and other forms of memory remain intact.
items.explanation: Debilitating means seriously weakening, so that a person cannot function as before. The sentence beginning “But” sets the patients against three healthy adults who “have always lacked that capacity yet function normally in everyday life.” For that contrast to work, losing the capacity must do patients real harm: it can be debilitating.

B.recipe: reversal: the trait of the wrong party (ANT)
B.why_wrong: Inconsequential means having little effect. That describes the three healthy adults, who “function normally in everyday life,” not the patients; the sentence beginning “But” sets the two groups against each other, so for the patients the loss must have serious effects.

C.why_wrong: Hereditary means passed down from parents to children. The text says nothing about whether the patients’ loss is inherited, and the contrast introduced by “But” is about how well people “function,” not about where the condition comes from.

D.why_wrong: Reversible means able to be undone. The text gives no information about whether patients recover the capacity, and the healthy adults’ ability to “function normally in everyday life” would not contrast with a loss that can be undone.

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Palombo, Alain, Söderlund, Khuu and Levine 2015 (Neuropsychologia), Severely deficient autobiographical memory (SDAM) in healthy adults: A new mnemonic syndrome: deficits in recollection in association with brain disease have serious functional consequences, while little is known about healthy individuals; three healthy, high functioning adults with lifelong SDAM; learning and memory otherwise intact; they function normally in day-to-day life

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology, memory). Rebuilt in review: the first draft (super-recognizers, Russell, Duchaine and Nakayama 2009) was judged a famous subject (popular label, viral online tests, police units). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (the But sentence sets healthy adults who function normally against the patients, so for patients the loss must impair functioning). Wrong-party trap: inconsequential is the healthy adults’ trait, as commonplace is the finding’s trait in 3.10. Raw freq.txt ranks: debilitating 56,950; inconsequential 34,175; hereditary 9,784; reversible 73,521. Crippling, disabling and devastating were not offered (each would also fit). Kept to the abstract: serious functional consequences with brain disease (can be), lifelong deficit (always lacked), learning and memory otherwise intact, function normally in day-to-day life. Authors’ first names from Europe PMC (Daniela J. Palombo, Brian Levine).
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

band7.why: Band 6 by plan. debilitating 56,950, inconsequential 34,175, hereditary 9,784, reversible 73,521; two steps (the But sentence contrasts healthy adults who function normally with patients, so the blank is the patients’ harm), with the other party’s trait (inconsequential) as the trap, as in 3.10. Strong band 6.

fixes: topic fame: replaced super-recognizers (Russell, Duchaine, Nakayama 2009; popular label, viral online tests, police units, a well-read adult may know it) with severely deficient autobiographical memory in healthy adults (Palombo, Levine et al. 2015, PubMed abstract); claim withdrawn and new claim appended to claims.txt
new passage, options, key (A, debilitating), explanation, distractors, sources and notes; same template, tier and band; reviewer re-solved it blind after rewriting (one defensible answer)
register: new passage at 5.84 chars per word keeps the hard tier at CB 5.25 (the literary M1 item pulls the tier down)

items.passage: Commercial harvesting appears to have made Fritillaria delavayi, an alpine herb used in traditional Chinese medicine, less ______: by gathering the specimens they spot, collectors seem to have spared plants whose leaves blend into their surroundings, and Yang Niu, Martin Stevens, and Hang Sun found such color matching to be closest in the most intensively harvested populations.
items.explanation: Discernible means able to be seen or detected. Because collectors take “the specimens they spot,” they seem to have “spared plants whose leaves blend into their surroundings,” and the researchers found this matching “closest in the most intensively harvested populations.” Harvesting has thus made the herb harder to see: less discernible.

A.why_wrong: Efficacious means effective, as a medicine might be. The text mentions the herb’s use “in traditional Chinese medicine” but says nothing about harvesting changing how well it works; the change it describes is in how the leaves look against “their surroundings.”

B.recipe: near miss: wrong feature of coloring (CONNOT)
B.why_wrong: Variegated means marked with patches of different colors. The text is about leaf color, but the change it describes is how closely leaves match “their surroundings,” not whether each leaf has more or fewer patches of color.

D.why_wrong: Palatable means pleasant to taste or eat. Nothing in the text concerns the herb’s taste; the collectors’ choices depend on which plants they see, “the specimens they spot.”

band7_moves: negation hidden in a comparative (less ______), with no plain negator
clue a level more abstract than the key: a selection process (collectors take what they spot, so survivors blend in) rather than a statement that the plant is hard to see
same-topic trap rather than a near synonym of the key: variegated (leaf coloring, but patchiness rather than matching the background)
all four options past rank 16,000, three past 24,000; no negation-flip distractor

sources.what: PubMed abstract, Niu, Stevens and Sun 2020 (Current Biology), Commercial Harvesting Has Driven the Evolution of Camouflage in an Alpine Plant: Fritillaria delavayi, a herb used in traditional Chinese medicine; leaves match local backgrounds; degree of background matching correlates with harvest pressure, plants more cryptic in heavily collected populations; in a human search experiment, time to find plants influenced by concealment

items.notes: Subject: natural science (botany, evolution). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (collectors remove the plants they see, so harvesting leaves the well-matched ones; the blank, under less, names visibility). Concessive frame: no; hidden negation: yes (less). Raw freq.txt ranks: efficacious 28,684; variegated 24,242; discernible 16,348; palatable 26,502 (4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000; mean log10 4.37). Band-5 guard: clear. Conspicuous, detectable, visible and noticeable were not offered (each would also fit). ‘appears to’ and ‘seem to’ keep to the abstract’s ‘point to humans as driving’. The near miss variegated is from the key’s field (leaf coloring) rather than a near synonym of discernible.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?

band7.why: Recounted: efficacious 28,684, variegated 24,242, discernible 16,348, palatable 26,502 (4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000, mean log10 4.37; combined gate passes; band-5 guard clear, key the commonest). Negation hidden in a comparative (less ______) as in the B5 model d7807ec8 (less sanguine), and a two-step selection clue a level more abstract than the key. Variegated is a same-field CONNOT trap, not a near synonym; section 5 asks for one, but section 2 finds band-7 distractors do not get closer (6 of 33 band-7 items have three plainly unsupported distractors, d7807ec8 has none), and every visibility near synonym (conspicuous, visible, noticeable) would also fit, so a swap would add a second answer. Kept at band 7.

fixes: band7_moves: variegated relabelled as a same-topic trap, not a near synonym of the key (batch note); options kept, see band7

items.passage:
The following text is from Eric Walrond’s 1926 short story “The Wharf Rats.” Maffi, a young woman from Trinidad, lives in the household of Jean Baptiste, a St. Lucian immigrant to coastal Panama.

And Maffi was such a hardworking patois girl. From the break of day she’d be at the sink, brightening the tinware. It was she who did the chores which Madame congenitally shirked. And towards sundown, when the labor trains had emptied, it was she who <u>scoured</u> the beach for cockles for Jean Baptiste’s epicurean palate.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “scoured” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “scoured” means searched thoroughly. Maffi goes to the beach “for cockles,” shellfish to satisfy Jean Baptiste’s “epicurean palate,” so she is looking all over the beach for them. The cleaning she does is described separately, in the morning, when “she’d be at the sink, brightening the tinware.”

A.recipe: another sense of the target, primed by the scene (SENSE)
A.why_wrong: Scour can mean to clean by hard rubbing, and the excerpt does describe Maffi cleaning “at the sink, brightening the tinware.” But at sundown she is on the beach “for cockles,” so she is hunting for food, not rubbing the beach clean.

C.why_wrong: Scour can mean to wear away, as flowing water scours a channel. Maffi is a person looking for “cockles for Jean Baptiste’s epicurean palate,” not a current wearing down the beach.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Maffi protects the beach. She goes there “for cockles,” which means she is looking for something to bring back.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook 71465, Eric Walrond, Tropic Death (Boni and Liveright, 1926), story “The Wharf Rats”: the paragraph beginning “And Maffi was such a hardworking patois girl” (copied exactly; italics on patois dropped as in CB transcripts); Maffi described earlier as a Trinidad girl in the household of Jean Baptiste, a St. Lucian, at Coco Té near Colon

items.notes: Subject: literature (short story, 1926, public domain in the US). Key letter B. Band 6, like 3.11 (determine/Dictate): the excerpt primes the everyday sense of the target (sink, tinware, chores) a sentence before it is used in another sense. Distractors: two real senses of scour (scrub, erode) and one unsupported word. Raw freq.txt ranks: Scrubbed 21,964; Searched 1,279; Wore away 1,068 (phrase option mixed with single words, as in 1.56); Guarded 1,257. Excerpt 57 words; narration only, no dialect speech. Walrond and Tropic Death appear in no other item (grep of all skills).

band7.why: Band 6 by plan, like 3.11 (determine/Dictate): the excerpt primes the cleaning sense of scour (sink, tinware) a sentence before the searching sense, and two distractors are real senses of the target. Key Searched is an everyday word, so not band 7.

items.passage: Printing technology was hardly ______ in the Ottoman Empire when diplomat İbrahim Müteferrika’s Istanbul press issued its first publication in 1729: Hebrew-language books had been printed within the empire since approximately 1500, and other religious communities operated presses as well. Müteferrika’s distinction was being the first Muslim to print using movable Arabic type.
items.explanation: Unprecedented means never done before. The text explains that “Hebrew-language books had been printed within the empire since approximately 1500, and other religious communities operated presses as well,” so printing had existed in the empire for more than two centuries before 1729. It was therefore hardly unprecedented; what was new, the last sentence says, was that Müteferrika was “the first Muslim to print using movable Arabic type.”

A.why_wrong: Established means set up and lasting for a long time. Saying printing was “hardly” established would contradict the text, which says books “had been printed within the empire since approximately 1500.”

B.why_wrong: Lucrative means profitable. The text says nothing about whether printing earned money; the colon introduces how long printing had existed in the empire, not what it paid.

C.why_wrong: Mechanized means done by machines, a word that fits the subject of presses. But the evidence after the colon concerns how long books had been printed in the empire, which says nothing about whether printing was or was not done by machine.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Ibrahim Muteferrika: the printing press had been known in the Ottoman Empire since 1493 or 1504 in Hebrew characters; other communities operated presses; Müteferrika was the first Muslim to run a printing press with movable Arabic type; his press published its first book in 1729 (Istanbul)

items.notes: Subject: history (Ottoman print culture). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (negated frame: printing had existed for two centuries, so it was hardly new; the last sentence locates what was new). Raw freq.txt ranks: established 2,806; lucrative 23,461; mechanized unseen; unprecedented 14,344. Novel and new were not offered. ‘since about 1500’ rounds the source’s 1493 or 1504; the Aleppo Arabic-type press of 1706 to 1711, run by Christians, is consistent with ‘first Muslim’.

items.passage: Some of composer Undine Smith Moore’s choral compositions were ______ her teaching responsibilities. Appointed to the music faculty of Virginia State College in 1927, Moore was additionally assigned to direct the chorus of the college’s laboratory high school, and because that school’s budget was meager, she composed original pieces tailored to her students’ requirements.
items.explanation: An outgrowth of something is a result that develops naturally from it. The text explains that Moore was “assigned to direct the chorus of the college’s laboratory high school” and, “because that school’s budget was meager, she composed original pieces tailored to her students’ requirements.” Those choral compositions grew out of her teaching.

B.why_wrong: A departure from something is a break away from it. The text presents the music as part of Moore’s duties, pieces “tailored to her students’ requirements,” not as a turn away from teaching.

C.why_wrong: A prelude to something comes before it and introduces it. Moore wrote the music after she was appointed to the college faculty and “assigned to direct the chorus,” so it followed from her teaching rather than leading up to it.

D.why_wrong: A substitute for something takes its place. Nothing suggests that Moore composed instead of teaching; she wrote the pieces for the students in the chorus she was directing.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Undine Smith Moore: hired in 1927 to teach at Virginia State College; appointed director of the D. Webster Davis Laboratory High School chorus, and due to the school’s low budget wrote her own music to cater to the students’ needs

items.notes: Subject: humanities (music, composer and teacher). Key letter A. Steps: 1 (restatement through a cause: the school lacked money, so she wrote music for her students). Raw freq.txt ranks: an outgrowth of 46,141; a departure from 1,837; a prelude to 14,281; a substitute for 9,221. A result of and a product of were not offered (each would also fit). ‘Some of’ keeps to the source, which does not say how much of her music began this way.

items.passage: At the Dōjima rice exchange, which emerged in Osaka around 1700, futures contracts were called chōaimai, or “the rice trades on the book.” That designation suited agreements that were ______ physical rice: no grain was delivered even when a contract reached maturity; participants simply settled the difference between purchase and sale prices.
items.explanation: To be divorced from something is to be completely separated from it. The text says that with these contracts “no grain was delivered even when a contract reached maturity” and that “participants simply settled the difference between purchase and sale prices.” The agreements existed only “on the book,” separate from any physical rice.

A.why_wrong: Redeemable for means able to be exchanged for. The text says the opposite: “no grain was delivered even when a contract reached maturity,” so the agreements were never exchanged for rice.

B.why_wrong: The text does not compare the value of the agreements with the value of rice; it explains that participants “settled the difference between purchase and sale prices.”

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that anyone confused the contracts with rice. The name “the rice trades on the book” suggests that traders knew the contracts were only entries in a record.

sources.what: Springer book page, Takatsuki and Takayasu, Microstructure of the First Organized Futures Market: the Dojima rice exchange emerged in Osaka around the turn of the eighteenth century; no physical delivery of rice or rice certificate in the futures market even on the maturity date; trades settled by paying or receiving the difference in price; the futures trade was called Cho-Ai-Mai, literally ‘the rice trades on the book’

items.notes: Subject: social science (economic history). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (the name says the trade lived on paper; the colon clause shows no rice was ever delivered; the blank names that separation in a transferred sense). Raw freq.txt ranks: redeemable for unseen; valued above 1,443; divorced from 7,742; mistaken for 2,016. Separate from, detached from and independent of were not offered (each would also fit). The gloss copies the source’s literal translation.

items.passage: Because local newspapers scrutinize officials and publicize how public funds are spent, their closure can be ______ for a county’s finances. Analyzing municipal bond markets, Pengjie Gao, Chang Lee, and Dermot Murphy found that three years after a county lost a local newspaper, yields on its bonds had increased by 0.05 to 0.11 percentage points, elevating the county’s borrowing costs.
items.explanation: Detrimental means harmful. The text gives the reason, that newspapers “scrutinize officials and publicize how public funds are spent,” and then the consequence of losing one: bond yields “had increased by 0.05 to 0.11 percentage points, elevating the county’s borrowing costs.” Paying more to borrow harms a county’s finances.

A.why_wrong: Ruinous means causing complete ruin. The text reports an increase in yields of “0.05 to 0.11 percentage points,” a cost that is harmful but far from destroying a county’s finances.

C.why_wrong: Beneficial means helpful. The text shows the opposite: after a closure, yields rose, “elevating the county’s borrowing costs.”

D.why_wrong: Unpredictable means impossible to foresee. The text gives a clear reason to expect harm, the loss of a paper that would “scrutinize officials,” and reports a consistent rise in borrowing costs.

sources.what: Brookings summary of Gao, Lee and Murphy, Financing Dies in Darkness? The Impact of Newspaper Closures on Public Finance (published in the Journal of Financial Economics, 2020): three years after a newspaper closure, municipal bond yields in that county increase by 0.05 to 0.11 percentage points; the authors attribute this to less public information and officials no longer monitored as closely

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics, public finance). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (newspapers monitor officials; losing one raised borrowing costs; so a closure harms finances). Raw freq.txt ranks: ruinous 15,823; detrimental 28,955; beneficial 17,134; unpredictable 69,096. Harmful, damaging and costly were not offered. The near miss ruinous is ruled out by the modest size of the rise, which the text states.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Elinore Pruitt Stewart’s 1914 book Letters of a Woman Homesteader. Stewart, a homesteader traveling by wagon through unfamiliar Wyoming terrain with her young children, has become disoriented and, approaching sunset, has reached an extensive plateau with abundant grass.

[The grass] encouraged me because the horses need not suffer, and if I could make the scanty remnant of our lunch <u>do for</u> the children’s supper and breakfast, we could camp in comfort, for we had blankets. But we must find water.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “do for” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “do for” means serve as, or be good enough to count as. Stewart hopes to stretch “the scanty remnant of our lunch” so that it can be the children’s next two meals, and if she can, “we could camp in comfort.” The leftover lunch would serve as supper and breakfast.

B.why_wrong: Do for can mean to ruin or destroy, as when someone is said to be done for. Stewart is hoping the food will feed her children, not harm their meals; making it last is what would let them “camp in comfort.”

C.why_wrong: Do for can mean to keep house for someone. But the subject here is “the scanty remnant of our lunch,” which cannot keep house; Stewart is asking whether the food will be enough.

D.why_wrong: Do for can mean to provide for or manage, as in asking how one will do for food. But Stewart wants the leftover food itself to be the meals; the lunch cannot make arrangements for the “supper and breakfast.”

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook 16623, Elinore Pruitt Stewart, Letters of a Woman Homesteader (Houghton Mifflin, 1914), letter XXIV, A Little Romance: lost among the buttes on the way to Kate Higbee’s place with the children, she reaches a grassy plateau at sunset; the sentence beginning ‘That encouraged me because the horses need not suffer’ (copied exactly; ‘That’ replaced by the bracketed ‘[The grass]’)

items.notes: Subject: literature (letters, 1914). Key letter A. All three distractors are real senses of the phrase do for (ruin; keep house for; provide for), as in 2.8, where every option shares a frame. Excerpt 39 words plus a context line; the bracketed insertion follows CB practice (‘[the rose]’). Stewart and this book appear in no other item; Bridger Bench, her destination, is in Wyoming.

items.passage: Composer Suzanne Ciani used an early electronic instrument, the Buchla synthesizer, to create sound effects for television and radio commercials during the 1970s, working for companies such as Coca-Cola and AT&T. One of those effects proved especially ______: her sound of a bottle of Coca-Cola being opened and poured became one of her most widely recognized works.
items.explanation: Memorable means easy to remember. The text explains after the colon that Ciani’s sound of a bottle of Coca-Cola being opened and poured “became one of her most widely recognized works.” A sound that many people recognize is a memorable one.

A.why_wrong: Fleeting means lasting only a short time. The text gives no sign that the sound was quickly forgotten or soon dropped; it says the sound “became one of her most widely recognized works.”

B.why_wrong: Obscure means little known. That is the opposite of what the text says: the sound was one of Ciani’s “most widely recognized works.”

D.why_wrong: Expensive means costing a lot. The text gives no information about what the sound cost to make; it focuses on how widely the sound came to be recognized.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Suzanne Ciani: early success in the 1970s with electronic music and sound effects for films and television commercials; Buchla synthesizer; the sound of a bottle of Coca-Cola being opened and poured, used in radio and television commercials in the late 1970s, was one of her most widely recognized works

items.notes: Subject: humanities (music, sound design). Key letter C. Steps: 1 (widely recognized restates memorable). Raw freq.txt ranks: fleeting about 6,000; obscure 5,213; memorable 8,945; expensive 6,205 (one band). Familiar and recognizable were not offered.

items.passage: Sculptor Meta Vaux Warrick Fuller’s Ethiopia, created around 1921 for an exhibition celebrating immigrants’ contributions to American culture, ______ ancient Egyptian art. Its figure of an African woman rising from a mummy’s wrappings draws on Egyptian sculptural traditions to express the pride in African heritage that flourished during the Harlem Renaissance.
items.explanation: To echo something is to repeat or recall it. The second sentence says that the sculpture’s figure of a woman “rising from a mummy’s wrappings draws on Egyptian sculptural traditions.” A work that draws on those traditions echoes ancient Egyptian art.

A.why_wrong: To predate something is to come before it. A sculpture “created around 1921” cannot have come before ancient Egyptian art.

B.why_wrong: To reject something is to refuse it. The text says the opposite: the sculpture “draws on Egyptian sculptural traditions.”

C.why_wrong: To conceal something is to hide it. Nothing suggests that Fuller’s sculpture hides Egyptian art; it borrows openly from it, showing a woman “rising from a mummy’s wrappings.”

sources.what: Wikipedia, Meta Vaux Warrick Fuller: Ethiopia (also known as Ethiopia Awakening), for the America’s Making Exhibition in 1921; drawn from Egyptian sculptural concepts, an African woman emerging from a mummy’s wrappings; represented the pride of African Americans in African and Black heritage; associated with the Harlem Renaissance

items.notes: Subject: humanities (sculpture). Key letter D. Steps: 1 (draws on Egyptian traditions restates echoes). Raw freq.txt ranks: predates unseen; rejects 11,839; conceals 3,228; echoes 4,393. Recalls and evokes were not offered.

items.passage: Esteban de Dorantes, a man from Azemmour, Morocco, was one of only four survivors of a Spanish expedition that landed in Florida in 1528. As the survivors journeyed westward across North America, Esteban often ______ his companions: having learned some of the Indigenous languages spoken along their route, he traveled in advance of the other three.
items.explanation: To precede someone is to go before them. The colon introduces what Esteban did: “he traveled in advance of the other three.” Going ahead of his companions means he preceded them.

B.why_wrong: To trail someone is to follow behind them. The text says the opposite: Esteban “traveled in advance of the other three.”

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that Esteban distrusted his companions; it explains only where he walked in relation to them and why.

D.why_wrong: To desert someone is to leave them for good. Esteban went ahead of the others but remained one of the four survivors traveling together; the text does not say he left them behind.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Esteban de Dorantes (Estevanico): native of Azemmour, Morocco; one of the four survivors of the Narváez expedition, which landed in Florida in 1528; in the Relación, Cabeza de Vaca said Esteban often went in advance of the other three survivors because he had learned some parts of the Indigenous language

items.notes: Subject: history (exploration). Key letter A. Steps: 1 (traveled in advance restates preceded). Raw freq.txt ranks: preceded 7,223; trailed 3,143; doubted 394; deserted 2,227. Led was not offered (it would also fit).

items.passage: The first images from Solar Orbiter, a spacecraft launched in 2020, revealed that tiny solar flares nicknamed “campfires” are ______ near the Sun’s surface. “The Sun might look quiet at the first glance,” said solar physicist David Berghmans, “but when we look in detail, we can see those miniature flares everywhere we look.”
items.explanation: Widespread means found over a large area. Berghmans explains that when the scientists “look in detail,” they “can see those miniature flares everywhere we look.” Flares that appear everywhere are widespread.

A.why_wrong: Immobile means unable to move. The text says nothing about whether the campfires move; Berghmans’s point is how many places they can be seen.

C.why_wrong: Scarce means hard to find. The text says the opposite: the scientists “can see those miniature flares everywhere we look.”

D.why_wrong: Permanent means lasting forever. Nothing in the text concerns how long each campfire lasts; it describes where they can be seen.

sources.what: ESA press release, 16 July 2020, Solar Orbiter’s first images reveal ‘campfires’ on the Sun: omnipresent miniature solar flares dubbed campfires near the Sun’s surface; Solar Orbiter launched 10 February 2020; quotation of David Berghmans (Royal Observatory of Belgium, principal investigator of the EUI instrument), given word for word

items.notes: Subject: natural science (astronomy). Key letter B. Steps: 1 (everywhere we look restates widespread). Raw freq.txt ranks: immobile about 8,000; widespread 20,619; scarce 2,797; permanent 6,682. Common and abundant were not offered. The quotation is copied exactly from the ESA release.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Yone Noguchi’s 1902 novel The American Diary of a Japanese Girl. The narrator, a young woman from Japan visiting the United States, is attending an afternoon tea hosted by her new acquaintance Ada.

I told about the horror of a certain famous Japanese earthquake. They all breathed out “Good heavens!”

There was one second of silence.

Ada <u>struck</u> a gushing melody on the piano.

The lively Meriken [American] ladies prompted themselves to frisk about.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “struck” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “struck” means played. Ada strikes “a gushing melody on the piano,” and the ladies then begin “to frisk about,” or dance, to the music. She played a tune to end the awkward “second of silence.”

A.why_wrong: Struck can mean impressed, as in being struck by an idea, but a melody is not impressed; Ada makes music “on the piano.”

B.why_wrong: Struck can mean discovered, as when someone strikes gold, but Ada does not find a melody; she performs one “on the piano” so that the ladies can dance.

D.why_wrong: Struck can mean removed, as when a word is struck from a list, but Ada adds music to the party rather than taking something away; the ladies begin “to frisk about.”

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook 63256, Yone Noguchi (as Miss Morning Glory), The American Diary of a Japanese Girl (Frederick A. Stokes, 1902): the tea at Ada’s, lines from ‘I told about the horror’ to ‘prompted themselves to frisk about’ (copied exactly, one gloss added)

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1902). Key letter C. All three distractors are other senses of struck (impressed, discovered, removed), as in 1.19. The diary prints each sentence as its own paragraph; the line breaks are kept. ‘[American]’ glosses the narrator’s spelling Meriken, so the source line says adapted. Yone Noguchi (the novelist) is the father of the sculptor Isamu Noguchi, who appears in other items; this is a different person and work.

items.passage:
The following text is from Jane Barlow’s 1896 short story “Mrs. Martin’s Company.” A mysterious plant growing inside the cottage of Mrs. Martin, an elderly widow in rural Ireland, has turned her home into a popular destination for visitors.

So many people now turned down the lane that they soon <u>wore</u> a track, which you could see distinctly if you looked along a stretch of its grass-grown surface. The Doctor came, and the District-Inspector, and the Protestant clergyman.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “wore” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “wore” means made by repeated use. So many visitors “turned down the lane” that their footsteps created a path, a track “which you could see distinctly” in the lane’s “grass-grown surface.” They made a track by walking it again and again.

B.why_wrong: Wore can mean displayed, as when someone wears a smile, but the visitors are not showing off a track; their walking produces one “which you could see distinctly.”

C.why_wrong: Wore can mean exhausted, as in wearing someone out, but the track did not exist before the visitors came; their many trips “down the lane” created it.

D.why_wrong: Wear can mean to last or hold up, but the text is not about the visitors putting up with a track; it says their many trips produced a path in the “grass-grown surface.”

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook 79670, Jane Barlow, Mrs. Martin’s Company and Other Stories (New York: Macmillan, 1896), title story: the sentences beginning ‘So many people now turned down the lane’ (copied exactly); Mrs. Martin, the ‘Widdy Martin’, a lonely old woman whose house draws visitors once a creeper grows round her image of the Virgin

items.notes: Subject: literature (short story, 1896). Key letter A. All three distractors are other senses of wear (display, tire out, last). Barlow and this collection appear in no other item.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Rolf Boldrewood’s 1888 novel Robbery Under Arms. The narrator describes a small settlement near the farm in Australia where he spent his childhood.

This village, like most of these places, had a public-house and a blacksmith’s shop. That was about all. The publican [tavern keeper] <u>kept</u> the store, and managed pretty well to get hold of all the money that was made by the people round about, that is of those that were ‘good drinking men’.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “kept” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Here “kept” means ran, or managed as a business. The publican was in charge of the village store and “managed pretty well to get hold of all the money that was made by the people round about.” He ran the store.

A.why_wrong: Kept can mean saved, as in keeping something for later, but the text describes the publican doing business at the store, getting “all the money that was made by the people round about.”

B.why_wrong: Kept can mean delayed, as in keeping someone waiting, but nothing in the text suggests the store was held up; the publican was making money from it.

C.why_wrong: Kept can mean obeyed, as in keeping a promise or a rule, but a store is not a promise or rule; the publican was running a business in the village.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg eBook 1198, Rolf Boldrewood, Robbery Under Arms (1888 book edition), chapter on the narrator’s boyhood: the sentences beginning ‘This village, like most of these places’ (copied exactly, one gloss added)

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1888). Key letter D. All three distractors are other senses of keep (save, detain, obey). ‘[tavern keeper]’ glosses publican, so the source line says adapted. The earlier sentence with ‘a school kept by an old chap’ is left out so that the target appears once. Boldrewood and this novel appear in no other item.

items.passage: Guatemalan American labor organizer Luisa Moreno, who led union campaigns among cannery workers in California, was largely ______ El Congreso de Pueblos de Habla Española (the Spanish-Speaking Peoples’ Congress). Requesting a leave of absence from her union post, she traveled to Los Angeles to organize the 1939 gathering, the first national Latino civil rights conference held in the United States.
items.explanation: To be responsible for something is to be the person who made it happen. The second sentence explains that Moreno took leave from her job and “traveled to Los Angeles to organize the 1939 gathering.” As its main organizer, she was largely responsible for El Congreso.

A.why_wrong: Moreno did not work against the conference; she took a leave from her job “to organize the 1939 gathering.”

C.why_wrong: The text presents Moreno as the one who brought the conference about, not as someone who drew inspiration from it after the fact; she went “to organize the 1939 gathering.”

D.why_wrong: To be unacquainted with something is to know nothing of it. Moreno organized the conference herself, so she could not have been unfamiliar with it.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Luisa Moreno: Guatemalan American labor and civil rights activist; primary organizer behind El Congreso de Pueblos de Habla Española, the first national Latino civil rights conference held in the United States; took a leave of absence and traveled to Los Angeles, where it was held April 28 to 30, 1939; organized cannery workers throughout California for UCAPAWA

items.notes: Subject: history (labor and civil rights). Key letter B. Steps: 1 (organized the gathering restates responsible for). Raw freq.txt ranks: opposed to 6,009; responsible for 3,178; inspired by 3,563; unacquainted with 21,980. Behind was not offered.

items.passage: In 1944 sculptor Selma Burke completed a relief portrait of President Franklin D. Roosevelt based on sketches she made during a sitting at the White House. Many people believe that engraver John R. Sinnock’s image of Roosevelt on the US dime was ______ Burke’s portrait, though Sinnock denied the connection and pointed to his own earlier medals depicting the president.
items.explanation: To be modeled on something is to be designed by copying or following it. The belief in the blank is something Sinnock “denied,” calling attention instead to “his own earlier medals depicting the president.” So the belief must be that his dime image was based on Burke’s portrait: modeled on it.

A.why_wrong: Unrelated to means having no connection with. That is Sinnock’s own position, but the text says he “denied the connection” that many people believe in, so the belief must be that a connection exists.

B.why_wrong: The text does not say where Sinnock’s dime image was shown; the dispute it describes is about whether his image was based on Burke’s portrait or on “his own earlier medals.”

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns money paid for either work; the disagreement is about the source of Sinnock’s image.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Selma Burke: 1944 plaque honoring Franklin D. Roosevelt, created from sketches made during a sitting at the White House; a number of sources contend that John R. Sinnock’s dime design was adapted from Burke’s plaque, though Sinnock denied it, pointing to his earlier presidential medals

items.notes: Subject: humanities (sculpture, coin design). Key letter C. Steps: 1 (Sinnock denied the connection, so the belief is that a connection exists). Raw freq.txt ranks: unrelated to 40,068 (modern word); displayed beside 4,640; modeled on 3,427; funded by 7,219. Based on and adapted from were not offered.

items.passage: A snake’s body temperature depends on its surroundings, which limits how large a snake can grow in a cool climate. That is why the 13-meter-long fossil snake Titanoboa, discovered in Colombia, allowed paleontologist Jason Head and colleagues to ______ the region’s climate roughly 60 million years ago: a snake that size would have required an average yearly temperature of at least 30–34°C.
items.explanation: To estimate something is to make a careful judgment about its size or amount. Because a snake’s size depends on how warm it is around it, the researchers could reason from Titanoboa’s size to the climate: “a snake that size would have required an average yearly temperature of at least 30–34°C.” The fossil let them estimate the region’s ancient climate.

B.why_wrong: To disrupt something is to throw it into disorder. A fossil found millions of years later could not have disturbed the climate “roughly 60 million years ago.”

C.why_wrong: The researchers did not ignore the climate; they used the snake’s size to work out that the region needed “an average yearly temperature of at least 30–34°C.”

D.why_wrong: To inflate something is to make it seem larger or higher than it is. Nothing in the text suggests the researchers overstated the climate’s warmth; the figure they give follows from the snake’s size.

sources.what: Nature abstract, Head et al. 2009, Giant boid snake from the Palaeocene neotropics reveals hotter past equatorial temperatures: Cerrejón Formation, northeastern Colombia, 58 to 60 million years ago; estimated body length 13 m; maximum size of poikilothermic animals at a given temperature is limited by metabolic rate, and a snake of this size would require a minimum mean annual temperature of 30 to 34 °C

items.notes: Subject: natural science (paleontology, climate). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (a snake’s size depends on warmth, so a giant snake implies a hot climate; the blank names reasoning from one to the other). Raw freq.txt ranks: estimate 5,499; disrupt 66,226 (modern word, easy); ignore 8,698; inflate about 9,000. Calculate and infer were not offered. Later critics questioned the method; the passage reports what Head and colleagues proposed, not that it is settled.

items.passage: Sculptor Martin Puryear, who studied biology and painting before turning to sculpture, is known for wooden works that reveal how they were constructed. Long before his career began, the objects he crafted by hand were remarkably ______: growing up in Washington, DC, he made guitars, canoes, and furniture.
items.explanation: Varied means of many different kinds. The colon introduces examples of what Puryear made as a young man: “guitars, canoes, and furniture.” A musical instrument, a boat, and household furniture are very different objects, so his handmade work was varied.

A.why_wrong: Repetitive means doing the same thing again and again. The examples show the opposite: Puryear made objects as different as “guitars, canoes, and furniture.”

B.why_wrong: Profitable means earning money. The text says nothing about Puryear selling what he made; it lists the kinds of objects he made.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that the objects or the work were dangerous; the examples show only the range of things Puryear crafted.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Martin Puryear: born in Washington, DC; began exploring traditional craft methods in his youth, making guitars, canoes, and furniture; studied biology, then art with a focus on painting, then an MFA in sculpture at Yale; works primarily in wood; known for visibly complex craft construction

items.notes: Subject: humanities (sculpture, craft). Key letter C. Steps: 1 (three unlike objects instantiate varied). Raw freq.txt ranks: repetitive unseen (modern, easy); profitable 8,932; varied 5,463; dangerous 1,553. Diverse and wide-ranging were not offered.

items.passage: Many works in Cuban American artist Ana Mendieta’s Silueta series (1973–1985) are outlines of a female figure made from ______ materials. Mendieta shaped these silhouettes, based on her own body, in mud, sand, and grass, and she sometimes formed them from leaves and twigs, recording these ephemeral works in photographs and film.
items.explanation: Natural materials are ones found in nature rather than made by people. The second sentence lists what Mendieta used: “mud, sand, and grass” and “leaves and twigs.” All of these come straight from the earth, so the materials are natural.

A.why_wrong: Costly means expensive. Nothing suggests that “mud, sand, and grass” or “leaves and twigs” cost much; they are found outdoors.

B.why_wrong: Synthetic means made by people, often by chemical processes. The examples are the opposite: “mud, sand, and grass” and “leaves and twigs.”

C.why_wrong: Uniform means all the same. The text lists several different materials, from “mud” to “twigs,” so the materials were not all alike.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Ana Mendieta: Cuban American artist; Silueta series (1973 to 1985), female silhouettes made in nature, in mud, sand, and grass, with natural materials ranging from leaves and twigs to blood; outlines of her own body; the Siluetas survive as films and photographs

items.notes: Subject: humanities (art). Key letter D. Steps: 1 (the listed materials instantiate natural). Raw freq.txt ranks: costly 1,508; synthetic 40,780 (modern, easy); uniform 4,122; natural 688. Organic and earthen were not offered.

items.passage: The Denmark Strait overflow, an enormous underwater current of frigid, dense water between Greenland and Iceland, descends more than three times as far as Venezuela’s Angel Falls. Unlike that waterfall, however, the overflow cannot be ______ from the shoreline or from a ship’s deck: its entire cascade occurs far beneath the ocean’s surface.
items.explanation: To observe something is to see or watch it. The text explains that the overflow’s “entire cascade occurs far beneath the ocean’s surface,” so a person on “the shoreline” or on “a ship’s deck” cannot see it. Unlike Angel Falls, it cannot be observed from there.

A.why_wrong: To foresee something is to know in advance that it will happen. The text is about where the cascade takes place, “far beneath the ocean’s surface,” not about whether anyone can predict it.

C.why_wrong: To imitate something is to copy it. Nothing in the text concerns copying the overflow; the contrast with Angel Falls is about where each can be seen from.

D.why_wrong: To avoid something is to keep away from it. The text does not suggest that anyone on a ship is trying to stay clear of the overflow; it explains that the cascade is hidden “far beneath the ocean’s surface.”

sources.what: Wikipedia, Denmark Strait overflow (also called the Denmark Strait cataract): undersea overflow between Greenland and Iceland; cold, dense water cascades along the seafloor; if on land it would be the tallest waterfall in the world, over three times the height of Angel Falls

items.notes: Subject: natural science (oceanography). Key letter B. Steps: 1 (negated frame: the cascade is under the sea, so it cannot be seen from above). Raw freq.txt ranks: foreseen about 9,000; observed 974; imitated about 9,000; avoided 2,101. Seen, spotted and photographed were not offered (each would also fit).
